claims.text: The system consists of sub-10 nm equiatomic Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles in vacuum.
Heating is performed from room temperature to 1000 K in vacuum.
The sluggish-diffusion assumption breaks down below a critical particle size of 5 nm.
Surface-energy minimization drives rapid Ostwald ripening in particles below the critical size.
Surface-energy minimization drives shape anisotropy in particles below the critical size.
Ostwald ripening causes the loss of the smallest particles.
Smaller particles dissolve while larger particles grow to reduce total surface free energy.
Surface-energy-driven segregation and Ostwald ripening dominate over bulk sluggish diffusion.
Heating to 1000 K will rapidly remove particles smaller than 5 nm.
Heating will shift the particle-size distribution toward larger particles.
The larger particles may become faceted.
A stable single-phase high-entropy structure will not be observed at 1000 K.
The theoretical baseline predicts a stable single-phase structure maintained by sluggish diffusion and high configurational entropy.
The proposed surface-energy-dominated regime applies to particles below 10 nm.
Larger particles may exhibit sluggish-diffusion behavior.
The exact critical size for the transition to surface-energy-dominated kinetics is unknown.
Whether segregation proceeds by core-shell formation or another phase-separation pathway is uncertain.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis places breakdown of sluggish diffusion below 5 nm, whereas the boundary states that the hypothesis applies to all particles below 10 nm. The behavior predicted for the 5–10 nm interval is therefore internally ambiguous.
